error_modes.label: Altitude holding while re-planning the profile

texts.0: SP, due to an instrument cross-check that stopped while SP re-sequenced the maneuvers of the profile, did not hold the planned altitude of the working block. The deviation passed 300 feet with a continuing trend and the formation approached the lower vertical limit of the assigned area. The IP intervened and returned the flight inside the block before the exercise was resumed.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow scan between the outside picture of the wingman and the altimeter, let the altitude drift while adjusting the maneuver sequence. The deviation stopped exactly at the 300 feet limit and was recognized only after the IP prompted verbally. The correction back to the planned altitude was made late and with an overshoot in the opposite direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed pitch correction while deciding on the next maneuver, allowed the altitude to move to about 200 to 250 feet from the planned value. SP detected the deviation, applied a smooth correction and re-established the flight inside 150 feet in good time. No intervention was required from the IP.
texts.3: SP planned the profile in flight while holding the planned altitude within 150 feet throughout. Every altitude change he ordered was flown to the new value accurately and the working block limits were respected at all times. Corrections were small, prompt and made without disturbing the wingman.
texts.4: SP held the planned altitude with deviations of the order of 50 feet during the whole in flight planning task. Level changes were anticipated, flown precisely and terminated on the assigned value. The vertical limits of the area were used with a clear margin at every stage of the profile.
texts.marginal: SP remained inside the altitude standard but worked repeatedly near the 150 feet edge, mostly on the high side, whenever he was re-planning the maneuver sequence. The corrections were correct but always started late and were larger than the deviation required. He is expected to protect the altitude cross-check while thinking ahead, so that the working deviation returns to the middle of the tolerance.

texts_at.0: SP replanned the profile in flight with the altitude cross-check talked through by the IP as each new maneuver was chosen, because this is SP's first in-flight replanning task at this stage and protecting the altimeter cross-check while thinking ahead has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to protect the altitude cross-check while re-sequencing without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP held the working altitude to about 300 feet from the planned value, at the tolerance limit, because the scan stayed on the maneuver sequence longer than the altimeter cross-check allowed before IP prompted the correction. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to protect the altitude cross-check while re-sequencing so the deviation does not run to the edge of the tolerance.
texts_at.2: SP let the altitude drift about 200 feet from the planned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the pitch correction was delayed while the next maneuver was being decided. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the pitch correction as soon as the deviation is seen rather than after the next maneuver is chosen.
texts_at.3: SP held the planned altitude within 150 feet while re-planning the profile on three of the four maneuvers, the fourth needing a slightly larger correction after a level change ordered a beat later than ideal. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same margin on every maneuver that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP held the working altitude to about 300 feet from the planned value, at the tolerance limit, once the deviation was cross-checked against the altimeter. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP caught the altitude moving toward 200 feet from the planned value and applied a smooth correction without prompting, re-establishing the level before it affected the block. Applying the correction as soon as the trend is seen, rather than once the next maneuver is chosen, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady altitude discipline while re-planning the profile.
texts_above.3: SP planned the profile in flight while holding the planned altitude within 150 feet throughout, with every level change flown accurately and corrections kept small, prompt and unobtrusive to the wingman. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate altitude discipline while re-planning the profile.
texts_above.4: SP held the planned altitude with deviations of the order of 50 feet during the whole in flight planning task, anticipating every level change and using the vertical limits of the area with a clear margin at every stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude discipline while re-planning the profile.

error_modes.label: Airspeed and energy management as leader

texts.0: SP, due to power changes made without reference to the airspeed indicator while adapting the profile, did not conserve the energy planned for the maneuver. The airspeed error passed 20 knots and left the wingman unable to hold position without large throttle excursions. The IP took over the energy management and re-established the entry parameters of the exercise.
texts.1: SP, due to a power setting selected late for a maneuver just decided on, allowed the airspeed to reach the 20 knots limit from the planned entry speed. SP restored the speed only after the IP called it, and the entry to the next maneuver was flown with the formation still accelerating. The energy loss forced an unplanned repositioning before the profile could continue.
texts.2: SP, due to a small delay in the power correction while revising the maneuver sequence, let the airspeed move about 12 to 18 knots from the planned value. SP identified the trend without prompting, corrected with a smooth throttle input and returned inside 10 knots before the entry of the maneuver. The wingman held position throughout without an excessive power demand.
texts.3: SP managed the energy of the formation so that the airspeed stayed within 10 knots of the planned value at every entry and exit of the profile. Power changes were made early, progressively and in a size that the wingman could match. Fuel was conserved as briefed while the sequence was adapted in flight.
texts.4: SP flew the whole revised profile with airspeed deviations of a few knots only, and every maneuver was entered at the planned energy state. Power was applied ahead of the demand so that the wingman never had to use large throttle corrections. The energy plan of the sortie was preserved without any loss of maneuver quality.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the 10 knots standard but consistently on the low side at the entry of each maneuver, so the margin for the wingman was thin. Each correction was adequate but was applied only when the deviation had already become visible in the formation. He is expected to lead the power change rather than follow the speed error, so that entry speeds sit on the planned value.

texts_at.0: SP managed the energy of the formation while replanning with the power setting for each new maneuver talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first in-flight replanning task at this stage and setting the power as soon as the next maneuver is chosen has not yet formed. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to set the power as soon as the next maneuver is chosen without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP let the airspeed reach about 20 knots from the planned entry value, at the tolerance limit, because the power setting for the newly chosen maneuver was selected late. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the power as soon as the next maneuver is chosen rather than after the airspeed has already moved.
texts_at.2: SP held the airspeed to no more than 15 knots off the planned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the power correction lagged slightly while the maneuver sequence was being revised. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to correct the airspeed as the sequence is revised rather than after the deviation is visible.
texts_at.3: SP held the airspeed within 10 knots of the planned value at the entry and exit of the profile on three of the four maneuvers, the fourth needing a small correction after a power change applied a moment late. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to time that one power change as precisely as the other three.

error_modes.label: Exit heading accuracy on the re-planned sequence

texts.0: SP, due to rolling out on an outside reference instead of the planned heading, did not exit the turn on the heading required by the revised sequence. The error passed 10 degrees and pointed the formation towards the lateral limit of the assigned area. The IP directed the correcting turn and re-established the axis of the next maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll out started after the planned heading had already passed, finished the maneuver with an exit heading error at the 10 degrees limit. The heading was corrected only after the IP pointed it out, and the wingman had to follow a second unbriefed turn. The next maneuver was entered displaced from the planned axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a late anticipation of the roll out while selecting the next maneuver, exited the turn about 7 degrees from the planned heading. SP recognized the error immediately, corrected with a shallow and predictable turn and re-established the heading within 5 degrees. The wingman remained in position during the correction.
texts.3: SP exited every turn of the adapted profile within 5 degrees of the planned heading. The roll out was anticipated so that each maneuver started on the intended axis inside the assigned area. The wingman was able to hold position without any additional correcting turn.
texts.4: SP established the exit heading of each maneuver on the planned value with a negligible error and without any secondary correction. The axis of the profile remained exactly as re-planned, well inside the lateral limits of the area. Every turn was terminated smoothly and predictably for the wingman.
texts.marginal: SP held the exit headings inside the 5 degrees standard but always with the same bias, rolling out slightly past the planned value on turns in one direction. The errors were small and corrected, yet they accumulated over the sequence and moved the working axis towards one side of the area. He is expected to anticipate the roll out earlier so that the exit heading is achieved without a follow up correction.

texts_at.0: SP exited the turns of the re-planned sequence with the roll-out point talked through by the IP as each new maneuver was chosen, because this is SP's first in-flight replanning task at this stage and anticipating the roll-out on a newly chosen axis has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to anticipate the roll-out on the re-planned axis without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP exited the turn about 10 degrees off the planned heading, at the tolerance limit, because the roll out was started only after the planned heading had already passed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the roll out on the re-planned axis rather than starting it after the heading has passed.
texts_at.2: SP exited the turn about 7 degrees off the planned heading, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, because the roll out was anticipated late while the next maneuver was being selected. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fix the roll out point as soon as the next maneuver is chosen.
texts_at.3: SP exited every turn of the adapted profile within 5 degrees of the planned heading on three of the four maneuvers, the fourth needing a small correction after a roll out anticipated a fraction late. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the same precision on every turn that the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP exited the turn about 10 degrees off the planned heading, at the tolerance limit, once the roll-out was anticipated on the re-planned axis. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a roll out drifting toward 7 degrees from the planned heading and corrected it with a shallow turn the wingman could follow, without any prompting. Anticipating the roll out as soon as the next maneuver is chosen, rather than correcting it afterward, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid exit heading precision on the re-planned sequence.
texts_above.3: SP exited every turn of the adapted profile within 5 degrees of the planned heading, with the roll out anticipated so each maneuver started on the intended axis inside the assigned area. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate exit heading precision on the re-planned sequence.
texts_above.4: SP established the exit heading of each maneuver on the planned value with a negligible error and without any secondary correction, keeping the axis of the profile exactly as re-planned well inside the lateral limits. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding exit heading precision on the re-planned sequence.

error_modes.label: Adaptation of the mission profile to weather, fuel and time

texts.0: SP, due to mission completion bias in pressing on with the briefed profile after the working area had become unusable, did not adjust the mission profile to the meteorological conditions, the fuel and the time constraints. The formation entered the maneuver with insufficient vertical room and the resulting altitude error went beyond 300 feet. The IP terminated the maneuver, re-planned the remaining profile and recovered the flight.
texts.1: SP, due to a decision to continue the planned sequence despite a cloud base that no longer supported it, adapted the profile only after the IP stated that the maneuver could not be flown. The delayed decision left the altitude at the 300 feet limit at the entry and the maneuver had to be repeated. The time and fuel spent on the correction were taken from the remaining objectives of the mission.
texts.2: SP, due to a late assessment of the weather and fuel picture, started the change of the maneuver sequence later than required. SP recognized the constraint, selected an alternative maneuver appropriate to the conditions and flew the entry with an altitude error of about 200 feet, corrected in good time. The mission objectives were achieved without any intervention from the IP.
texts.3: SP adjusted the mission profile in flight in accordance with the meteorological conditions, the remaining fuel and the time available. The alternative maneuvers he selected served the mission objectives and were flown within 150 feet and 10 knots of the planned values. The decision was taken early enough for the wingman to be briefed before the change.
texts.4: SP anticipated the effect of the deteriorating conditions on the profile and re-planned the sequence before the constraint became limiting. The revised profile met every mission objective with precise parameters and an orderly use of the remaining fuel and time. No maneuver had to be repeated and the wingman was never surprised by a change.
texts.marginal: SP adapted the profile correctly to the conditions and the fuel state, but each decision was taken at the last usable moment and left little margin for the wingman. The parameters remained inside standards, although the entries were flown closer to the limits of the area than the situation required. He is expected to take the re-planning decision one maneuver earlier, so that the change is executed with a comfortable margin.

texts_at.0: SP adapted the mission profile to the weather and fuel picture with the constraint and the alternative maneuver talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first in-flight replanning task at this stage and recognizing a limiting constraint as it develops has not yet formed. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to make the adaptation decision as soon as the constraint is seen without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP adapted the profile only after IP stated that the maneuver could not be flown as briefed, and the altitude at the entry sat about 300 feet from the planned value, at the tolerance limit, while the decision was still being made. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to make the adaptation decision as soon as the constraint is seen rather than after IP states it.
texts_at.2: SP started the change of the maneuver sequence a little later than the weather and fuel picture required, and the entry altitude reached about 200 feet off the planned value, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the correction was made without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assess the weather and fuel picture earlier so the change is made before the constraint becomes limiting.
texts_at.3: SP adjusted the mission profile to the conditions and flew the resulting entries within 150 feet on three of the four maneuvers, the fourth needing a small correction after a decision taken a beat later than ideal. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to take that one decision with the same lead time the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP adapted the profile once the constraint was named, holding the entry altitude to about 300 feet from the planned value, at the tolerance limit, while the decision was made. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP started the change of the maneuver sequence a little later than the conditions required but recognized the constraint without prompting, selecting an alternative maneuver and flying the entry with the altitude held to about 200 feet. Assessing the weather and fuel picture earlier, rather than after the trend is visible, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable judgment in adapting the mission profile.
texts_above.3: SP adjusted the mission profile in flight to the meteorological conditions, the remaining fuel and the time available, flying the alternative maneuvers within 150 feet and 10 knots of the planned values with the wingman briefed before the change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good judgment in adapting the mission profile.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the effect of the deteriorating conditions and re-planned the sequence before the constraint became limiting, meeting every mission objective with precise parameters and no maneuver repeated. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior judgment in adapting the mission profile.

error_modes.label: Timing, fuel allocation and use of the assigned area

texts.0: SP, due to a sequence flown without reference to the timing agreed at the briefing, did not use the allocated fuel in accordance with the plan. The formation was still in the area with the fuel below the planned figure and the recovery had to be started immediately. The IP took the decision to leave the area and led the flight out of the vertical and lateral limits in a controlled manner.
texts.1: SP, due to repeating a maneuver rather than moving on with the time line, consumed the fuel margin planned for the remaining profile. The reallocation of the sequence was made only after the IP indicated the fuel and time state, and the last exercise was flown with the formation drifting to the 300 feet limit of the block. The mission was completed but without the reserve planned at the briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to a repositioning turn flown wider than necessary, lost part of the time allocated to the sequence. SP noticed the deviation from the briefed time line, shortened the following repositioning and completed the profile inside the assigned area with parameters within 150 feet and 10 knots. The fuel state at the end of the exercise matched the plan without any intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the profile on the time specified at the briefing and used the allocated fuel as planned. The maneuvers were positioned so that the formation remained inside the vertical and lateral limits of the assigned area at all times. The sequence was completed with the fuel state and the time line as briefed.
texts.4: SP conducted the sequence so that every maneuver was flown at its planned time with the fuel consumption matching the briefed profile. Repositioning was minimal and the area was used efficiently, with wide margins to the vertical and lateral limits. The formation left the area exactly on the planned time and fuel state.
texts.marginal: SP respected the time line and the fuel plan but with a working position close to one boundary of the assigned area for most of the sortie. Nothing exceeded the limits, although each repositioning had to be flown tighter than briefed to keep the sequence inside the area. He is expected to plan the geometry of the sequence at the start, so that timing and fuel are met from a central position in the block.

texts_at.0: SP timed the re-planned sequence against the fuel and the block with the time line talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first in-flight replanning task at this stage and checking the time line before repeating a maneuver has not yet formed. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to check the time line against the plan before repeating a maneuver without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP repeated a maneuver rather than moving on with the time line, and the last exercise was flown with the formation drifting to about 300 feet from the block limit, at the tolerance limit, before IP indicated the fuel and time state. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the time line against the plan before repeating a maneuver rather than after the fuel margin is already spent.
texts_at.2: SP flew a repositioning turn wider than necessary and lost part of the time allocated to the sequence, with the resulting altitude reaching about 200 feet from the block limit, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the following repositioning was shortened without prompting. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the repositioning turn correctly the first time rather than shortening the next one to compensate.
texts_at.3: SP executed the profile on the briefed time line and used the allocated fuel as planned on three of the four maneuvers, holding the block within 150 feet, with the fourth needing a small correction after a repositioning flown a touch wide. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size every repositioning turn as tightly as the first three.

texts_above.1: SP repeated a maneuver against the time line, holding the formation to about 300 feet from the block limit, at the tolerance limit, once the fuel and time state was named. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP lost part of the allocated time to a repositioning turn flown wider than necessary but noticed the deviation from the briefed time line without prompting, shortening the following repositioning and completing the profile with the block held to about 200 feet. Sizing the repositioning turn correctly the first time, rather than compensating on the next one, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured management of timing and fuel against the area.
texts_above.3: SP executed the profile on the time specified at the briefing and used the allocated fuel as planned, positioning the maneuvers so the formation remained inside the vertical and lateral limits of the area at all times. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise management of timing and fuel against the area.
texts_above.4: SP conducted the sequence so every maneuver was flown at its planned time with the fuel consumption matching the briefed profile, using the area efficiently with wide margins to the vertical and lateral limits. error_modes.label: Monitoring and control of the wingman position

texts.0: SP, due to an absent monitoring and cross-check of the wingman while concentrating on the maneuver, did not control and take into account No2 during the re-planned sequence. SP continued the maneuver without knowing the position of the wingman in space and the formation geometry broke down. The IP intervened, called the wingman clear and re-established the formation before the profile continued.
texts.1: SP, due to a check of No2 made only at the end of each maneuver, lost track of how the wingman was moving in space during the turns. SP corrected the geometry only after the IP called the position of No2, and the airspeed reached the 20 knots limit while the formation was being re-established. The wingman had to use large corrections to remain in place.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that gave priority to SP's own parameters at the entry of each maneuver, checked the wingman later than required. SP detected the developing spread, moderated the maneuver and re-established a workable geometry with the speed back inside 10 knots. The wingman remained in position and no intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP checked the position of No2 continuously and had a clear understanding of how the wingman was moving in space. He controlled the maneuvers so that the wingman could hold position with parameters inside 150 feet and 10 knots. Every change of the profile took account of the state of the wingman before it was flown.
texts.4: SP maintained an accurate picture of the wingman throughout the profile and adjusted each maneuver to what No2 could fly comfortably. The formation stayed consistent through every change of the sequence, with negligible parameter deviations on both aircraft. The wingman was never required to make a large correction to remain in place.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the wingman adequately but the checks were concentrated at the entries and exits, with long gaps during the body of each maneuver. The formation stayed consistent, although the geometry had to be recovered at the end of two maneuvers rather than being protected during them. He is expected to distribute the check of No2 through the whole maneuver, so that corrections are made while they are still small.

This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the wingman before settling the leader's own parameters at each entry.

error_modes.label: Formation consistency and break out decision

texts.0: SP, due to a decision to keep the formation together in conditions that no longer allowed visual contact to be maintained, did not break out when required by the manuals and the briefing. The wingman lost visual contact inside cloud with the flight still turning and the altitude error went beyond 300 feet. The IP ordered the break out and separated the aircraft in accordance with the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to a break out ordered after the visual contact had already become marginal, executed the separation late and without the geometry described in the briefing. The break out was initiated only on the prompt of the IP and the exit heading was left at the 10 degrees limit from the briefed separation heading. The rejoin afterwards consumed time and fuel that had been allocated to the profile.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly delayed recognition of the deteriorating visibility, held the formation together longer than the situation justified. SP then ordered the break out, flew the briefed separation heading within 7 degrees and kept the deconfliction as described in the manuals. The rejoin was completed without any intervention from the IP.
texts.3: SP kept the formation flexible and consistent through the changing external conditions and ordered the break out when the criteria of the briefing were met. The separation was flown on the briefed headings within 5 degrees and with the altitude split respected. The formation was rejoined in a controlled manner once conditions allowed.
texts.4: SP judged the changing conditions accurately, held a consistent formation while it was safe to do so and initiated the break out at exactly the point defined in the briefing. The separation was executed with precise headings and altitudes and no ambiguity for the wingman. The subsequent rejoin was smooth and cost nothing in time or fuel.
texts.marginal: SP maintained a consistent formation and made a correct break out decision, but the call was made at the last point where the manuals still permitted it. The execution met the standard, although the wingman had very little time to react to the separation. He is expected to set his break out trigger earlier against the deteriorating condition, so that the decision is taken with margin rather than at the limit.

texts_at.0: SP flew the break out with the separation heading and the trigger for the decision talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first break-out decision at this stage and recognizing marginal visual contact early has not yet formed. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to order the break out at the first sign of marginal visual contact without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP ordered the break out only on IP's prompt, after visual contact had already become marginal, and the exit heading was left about 10 degrees from the briefed separation heading, at the tolerance limit. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to order the break out at the first sign of marginal visual contact rather than after it has already degraded.
texts_at.2: SP held the formation together a little longer than the deteriorating visibility justified, then ordered the break out without prompting and flew the briefed separation heading to within 7 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize the deteriorating visibility as promptly as the break out itself was executed.
texts_at.3: SP kept the formation consistent through the changing conditions and ordered the break out when the briefing criteria were met on three of the four sorties, holding the briefed separation heading inside 5 degrees, the fourth showing a small delay in recognizing the trigger. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to recognize that trigger with the same promptness the first three showed.

texts_above.1: SP ordered the break out once prompted, flying the separation heading to about 10 degrees from the briefed value, at the tolerance limit, as visual contact was becoming marginal. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP held the formation together slightly longer than the deteriorating visibility justified but then ordered the break out without prompting, flying the briefed separation heading within 7 degrees and keeping the deconfliction as described in the manuals. Recognizing the deteriorating condition as promptly as the break out was executed, rather than after a short delay, would close that margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady judgment on formation consistency and break out.

error_modes.label: Positioning of No2 relative to the sun and the local area

texts.0: SP, due to a maneuver selected without considering the position of No2 in relation to the sun, placed the wingman looking directly into the sun during the turn. The wingman lost sight of the lead aircraft and the formation geometry was no longer controlled. The IP intervened, directed the lost wingman procedure and re-established the flight.
texts.1: SP, due to a turn direction chosen without reference to the sun and the local area, forced the wingman to hold position against a saturated visual background. SP reversed the direction only after the IP identified the problem, and during the reversal the airspeed reached the 20 knots limit. The wingman held position with difficulty and with large corrections.
texts.2: SP, due to a late assessment of the sun line relative to the working area, started the maneuver with the wingman in an unfavourable visual position. SP recognized the problem within the first part of the turn, adjusted the direction of the maneuver and restored a workable visual picture with parameters back inside 10 knots. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP took the position of No2 in relation to the sun and the local area into account and selected the appropriate maneuver each time. The wingman kept a clear visual reference throughout the profile and held position with deviations inside 150 feet and 10 knots. The geometry of the sequence was arranged so that no turn placed the wingman against the sun.
texts.4: SP planned the direction of every maneuver so that the wingman always had a favourable visual background against the sun and the terrain features of the area. The visual task of No2 remained easy through the whole revised profile and the formation stayed precise. No repositioning was ever needed for visual reasons.
texts.marginal: SP considered the sun position and selected acceptable maneuver directions, but on two turns the wingman was left with a marginal visual background for part of the arc. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior planning of No2's position against the sun.

Parameters on both aircraft remained inside 150 feet and 10 knots through the changes.
texts.4: SP passed clear and timely information for every change of the profile, so that the wingman knew what was coming and prepared for it. texts.3: SP remained predictable throughout the profile and his effect on the flight controls was smooth and progressive. The task was completed smoothly with parameters inside 150 feet, 10 knots and 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP flew every maneuver of the revised sequence with control inputs so smooth and predictable that the wingman required almost no correction to remain in place. error_modes.label: Clearing for the formation as the first responsibility of Number 1
error_modes.source: technique:9.3 RESPONSIBILITIES - FLIGHT LEADER, NUMBER 1 AND NUMBER 2

texts.0: SP, due to planning ahead of the A/C absorbing the whole scan, abandoned the first of the Number 1 basic responsibilities, which is to clear for the formation. SP re-sequenced the profile with attention inside the cockpit, ensured nobody was clearing and turned the flight into airspace not yet swept, while the altitude left the working block by more than 300 feet. The IP intervened, cleared the flight path and returned the formation inside the block before the sequence continued.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout compressed into the short gaps between re-planning tasks, left the formation unswept through the entries of two maneuvers. Clearing resumed only after a verbal prompt from the IP to clear before the turn, and the altitude reached the 300 feet limit while attention was in the cockpit. The priority order of clearing first and planning second was restored only after the reminder.
texts.2: SP, due to giving the re-sequencing of the profile priority over the lookout at the entry of each maneuver, cleared for the formation later than the situation required. SP recognized the omission, swept the flight path before the next turn and recovered the altitude from about 250 feet of drift back inside 150 feet. No prompting was required and the wingman remained in place.
texts.3: SP cleared for the formation before every change of direction and did his in flight planning within the time left by that priority. The flight path was swept ahead of each maneuver of the revised sequence and the parameters stayed inside 150 feet and 10 knots. The order of Number 1 responsibilities was respected throughout the profile.
texts.4: SP kept a continuous lookout for the formation and fitted the re-planning of the profile around it without any loss of coverage. Every maneuver of the revised sequence was entered into airspace he had already swept, with negligible deviations in altitude and airspeed. Clearing, planning and monitoring of No2 were sustained together for the whole exercise.
texts.marginal: SP cleared for the formation before each maneuver but the sweep was short and concentrated in the direction of the next turn, with the re-planning taking the rest of his attention. The flight path was adequately covered and the parameters remained inside standards. He is expected to widen the lookout and to break the planning into smaller pieces, so that clearing stays the leading task rather than the one that is squeezed.

texts_at.0: SP cleared for the formation while re-planning with the priority of clearing before planning talked through by the IP, because this is SP's first time balancing lookout against in-flight planning at this stage and the priority has not yet formed as a habit. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to clear for the formation before every turn without the reminder on the next sorties.
texts_at.1: SP resumed clearing only after IP prompted verbally to clear before the turn, and the altitude reached about 300 feet from the block, at the tolerance limit, while attention was in the cockpit. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to clear for the formation before every turn without needing the reminder.
texts_at.2: SP gave the re-sequencing of the profile priority over the lookout at the entry of a maneuver, and the altitude drifted to about 200 feet, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, before the omission was recognized and the flight path swept without prompting. texts_at.3: SP cleared for the formation before every change of direction and held the altitude within 150 feet on three of the four maneuvers, the fourth needing a small correction after a sweep that started a beat late. SP recognized the overlap, repeated the direction cleanly and had the flight together on the new frequency with deviations back inside 10 knots. The rest of the profile was run without any radio confusion.
texts.3: SP directed every frequency change himself and confirmed the check in of the wingman before continuing with the revised sequence. No frequency was changed in the formation without his direction, and the parameters stayed inside 150 feet and 10 knots through the changes. The wingman remained on frequency and in position throughout.
texts.4: SP retained full control of the radios of the formation, directing and confirming each change at a moment that did not compete with a maneuver. The wingman was always on the correct frequency and the flight never lost a transmission, with negligible parameter deviations during the changes. Radio management supported the profile instead of interrupting it.
texts.marginal: SP kept control of the radios and confirmed each check in, but the frequency changes were directed at busy points of the sequence and needed a second call twice. texts_at.3: SP directed every frequency change and confirmed the wingman's check-in within 10 knots of split on three of the four changes, the fourth check-in confirmed a moment later than ideal. texts.3: SP flew each high performance maneuver with smooth and deliberate control inputs, having considered the position of No2 and his ability to perform the maneuver safely. texts.0: SP, due to directing the ops check without allowing the wingman enough time to accomplish it, turned the formation while No2 was still working through the checklist. The IP intervened, stopped the check and re-established the formation before the mission continued.
